overview.body:
**Kérberos** (*cerberus*) — Underworld Guardian · The Hound of Hades, Warden of the Dead — is the monstrous watchdog of the Greek underworld: the brazen-voiced, many-headed hound who fawns on all who enter the house of Hades and devours any who try to leave.[^1]

Hesiod makes him the child of the monsters Typhoeus and Echidna, brother to the two-headed Orthrus, the Hydra, and the Chimaira — ‘a brazen-voiced hound of Hades, fifty-headed, relentless and strong’.[^1] His one starring episode is the last and hardest of the labours of Herakles, who dragged him in chains up from the underworld into the daylight; but his quieter role is older and more terrible: he is the boundary of death made animal, the one gatekeeper no prayer, bribe, or second thought can pass.[^2] Only song and honey-cakes ever moved him — Orpheus' lyre, the Sibyl's drugged sop.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Kérberos** and serves its temple at [kérberos.com](https://xn--krberos-bya.com). The restoration keeps the Greek kappa the Latin alphabet softened to C and the acute accent on the first syllable where Greek puts the stress; the plain ASCII *cerberus* is the Roman-mediated form, a technological and transliterational compromise rather than the Greek spelling.[^3]

sources.citation: Hesiod, Theogony 306–312, ed. and trans. Glenn W. Most, Loeb Classical Library (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2018).
Apollodorus, The Library 2.5.12 (the twelfth labour), trans. J. G. Frazer, Loeb Classical Library (1921).
Beekes, Robert, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Leiden: Brill, 2010), s.v. Κέρβερος.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Κέρβερος** (genitive Κερβέρου), accented on the first syllable. Its etymology is genuinely contested. An old Indo-European proposal connects it with Sanskrit *śárvara-* / *karbara-* ‘spotted, variegated’ — an epithet of one of Yama's two hounds of death in the Veda — which would make Kérberos ‘the spotted one’, a cousin of the Indian hell-hounds.[^1] A Greek folk etymology heard the name as *kreobóros*, ‘flesh-devouring’. Modern lexicography (Beekes) treats the word as probably Pre-Greek, a survival from the substrate language of the Aegean.[^2]

The familiar ASCII form *cerberus* is doubly mediated: Latin took the Greek Κέρβερος, wrote it *Cerberus* with Roman C and the Latin nominative -us, and English inherited the Roman spelling. The Unicode restoration **Kérberos** returns the Greek kappa, restores the omicron of the penult, and marks the accent — the form the name wears in Hesiod and Homer. Because the Greek original carries only the single feature of stress, without vowel length, the name is classified Tier 2 (accent-preserving).

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **c** → **K** — Greek kappa (Κ)
- **e** → **é** — Acute on e
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **b** → **b** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **u** → **o** — Greek omicron (Latin -u- for Greek -ο-)
- **s** → **s** — Same

The project holds the domain **kérberos.com** (xn--krberos-bya.com) as the canonical home of this name.

sources.citation: Lincoln, Bruce, Death, War, and Sacrifice: Studies in Ideology and Practice (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991), on the Indo-European hell-hound.
Beekes, Robert, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Leiden: Brill, 2010), s.v. Κέρβερος.
Liddell, Scott & Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1940), s.v. Κέρβερος.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈkér.be.ros/** — Classical Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Kér-** — Aspirated voiceless velar [kʰ], short front [e], trilled [r]; the acute accent marks the stressed first syllable
- **-be-** — Voiced bilabial stop [b] with short [e]
- **-ros** — Trilled [r], short back [o], voiceless [s]; the Greek nominative ending -ος that Latin rewrote as -us

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘KAIR-beh-ross’ — three crisp syllables, stress on the first, rolled r's.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Κέρβερος (Kérberos), the hound of Hades
- **Latin** — Cerberus, the Romanized form that passed into English
- **Vedic parallel** — Śarvara, ‘the spotted one’, epithet of a hound of Yama, the proposed cognate[^2]

Kérberos is Tier 2: the Greek original preserves the stress accent only. There is no vowel-length feature to restore; the accent and the kappa are the whole of what ASCII lost.

sources.citation: Allen, W. Sidney, Vox Graeca: A Guide to the Pronunciation of Classical Greek, 3rd ed. (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1987).
Lincoln, Bruce, Death, War, and Sacrifice (University of Chicago Press, 1991).

domains.body:
**Kérberos** is the watchdog of the dead: not a judge, not a punisher, but the boundary itself — the living gate through which the living may enter only on the rarest errands and the dead may never exit.[^1]

### Warden of the Threshold

Hesiod places him before the house of Hades and Persephone: he fawns with tail and ears on those who enter, but lets none out, watching the road and devouring whoever tries to pass back through the gate.[^1]

### Prize of Herakles

The twelfth labour made him the trophy of the greatest katabasis: brought up in chains to King Eurystheus, shown to the daylight, and returned below.[^2]

### Child of Monsters

Son of Typhoeus and Echidna, brother of Orthrus, the Hydra, and the Chimaira — the underworld branch of Greek myth's great monster-house.[^1]

### The Unbribable Gate

Song and honey-cake alone ever subdued him; he is death's refusal of negotiation given fur and fangs.

symbols.body:
The iconography of Kérberos concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The multiple heads** — Hesiod gives fifty; the classical and Roman imagination settled on three; vase painters often manage two, with serpents sprouting from mane and tail
- **The chain** — Herakles' instrument: the hound subdued not by sword (Herakles was forbidden weapons by Hades) but by wrestling and binding
- **The serpents** — A mane and tail of snakes, inheritance of his mother Echidna, half woman and half serpent
- **The honey-cake** — The Sibyl's drugged sop in the *Aeneid* and the cakes Psyche carries in Apuleius: the ancient passport of the living through the gate of the dead[^2]
- **The adamantine gate** — In Virgil he lies in a cave facing the threshold of Avernus' descent, the door of Dis itself

mythology.body:
Kérberos enters the written record fully formed in Hesiod's *Theogony*: the brazen-voiced, fifty-headed hound of Hades, offspring of Typhoeus and Echidna.[^1] A few hundred lines later Hesiod gives him his office, in one of the most quietly frightening passages of early Greek poetry — the hound who wags his tail and drops his ears for all who go down into the house of Hades, but eats anyone who tries to come back out.[^2]

### The Twelfth Labour (Homer to Apollodorus)

Homer already knows the hound's abduction: Athena in Iliad 8 reminds Zeus how often she saved Herakles in his labours for Eurystheus, ‘when he went down to the house of the door-keeper Hades to fetch the hound of hateful Hades from Erebos’; Odysseus in Odyssey 11 sees Herakles among the dead and recalls the same errand.[^3] Apollodorus tells the full story: guided by Hermes and Athena, Herakles descended — at Tainaron in the usual account — asked Hades for the hound, was granted him on condition of using no weapons, wrestled him at the gates of Acheron despite the bites of his serpent-tail, and carried him to Eurystheus at Mycenae, where the sight of the beast drove the king to hide in his bronze jar. The hound was then returned to the underworld.[^4]

### The Ones Who Passed (Orpheus, the Sibyl, Psyche)

Three later traditions record the hound's only defeats. Orpheus charmed him with the lyre on the descent for Eurydice — Virgil's *Georgics* has Kérberos hold his three gaping mouths in awe.[^5] The Sibyl in *Aeneid* 6 drugs him with a honey-cake steeped in soporific herbs, and he collapses across his cave. And Apuleius' Psyche, on her underworld errand for Venus, is instructed to carry two barley cakes soaked in honeyed wine — one for the way down, one for the way back, since the hound permits each traveller exactly one passage.[^6]

### The Boundary Itself

Across all versions the function is constant: Kérberos does not hunt the living and does not judge the dead. He simply guarantees the one-way door — the animal embodiment of the ancient world's most absolute law.

syncretism.body:
The Roman reception made him *Cerberus* — the form English inherited — and Roman poetry enlarged his stage: Virgil stations him in a cave before the very threshold of Dis, Horace calls him the hundred-headed beast, and Seneca's *Hercules Furens* dramatizes the descent.[^1] The comparative school of the twentieth century pressed further: Bruce Lincoln read Kérberos beside the Vedic hounds of Yama — the two spotted, four-eyed dogs Śyāma and Śabala who guard the road of the dead — arguing for an inherited Indo-European ‘hound of death’, of which the Greek hound and the Sanskrit *śárvara* epithet are cognate survivals.[^2]

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[hades|Hādēs]] (the master he serves), [[typhon|Typhôn]] (his father), [[herakles|Hēraklēs]] (the hero who bound him), and [[ker|Kēr]] (Greek death-spirits of the same threshold world).

sources.citation: Lincoln, Bruce, Death, War, and Sacrifice: Studies in Ideology and Practice (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1991).

cultural-legacy.body:
Kérberos outlived his cult to become the European archetype of the implacable guard. Dante set him over the third circle of the *Inferno*, a three-throated beast rending the gluttons, clawed red by the Florentine's imagination.[^1] Heraldry, proverb, and politics borrowed him for every door that must not be passed; ‘a Cerberus at the gate’ is still English shorthand for a hostile guardian.

Twentieth-century culture gave him two striking second lives. In computing, MIT's Kerberos network-authentication protocol was named for the three-headed hound — its three heads glossed as client, server, and the trusted ticket-granting service that guards the gate between them.[^2] And in children's literature he stands barely disguised at a third-floor door: Hagrid's three-headed dog Fluffy in *Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone*, lulled to sleep by music exactly as Orpheus taught.[^3]

sources.citation: Steiner, Jennifer G., Clifford Neuman, and Jeffrey I. Schiller, ‘Kerberos: An Authentication Service for Open Network Systems,’ Proceedings of the USENIX Winter Conference (1988).
Rowling, J. K., Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (London: Bloomsbury, 1997).

archaeology.body:
Kérberos had no cult and no temple; his material record is iconographic. Greek vase painting made the twelfth labour one of its favourite scenes: Athenian black-figure amphorae of the sixth century BCE show Herakles leading the two- or three-headed hound on its chain toward a shrinking Eurystheus, and a celebrated Laconian cup in the Cabinet des Médailles, Paris (c. 560 BCE), places the encounter among the earliest masterpieces of Spartan pottery.[^1] South Italian red-figure kept the theme through the fourth century, often within larger underworld tableaux.

The two descent-sites are the closest thing to his shrines. At Cape Tainaron in the Peloponnese, Pausanias saw the cave ‘through which, they say, Herakles brought up the hound of Hades’; at Herakleia Pontike on the Black Sea, Xenophon's Ten Thousand marched past the Acherusian promontory, ‘where they say the hound Cerberus was brought up’, its cavern plunging more than two stades into the earth.[^2]

sources.citation: Boardman, John, Athenian Black Figure Vases (London: Thames and Hudson, 1974), on the Herakles-and-Kerberos scenes.
Pausanias, Description of Greece 3.25.5–6; Xenophon, Anabasis 6.2.2.

meditation.body:
Kérberos is the shape a culture gives to the one boundary it cannot negotiate. The Greeks let their heroes do almost everything — defy gods, sack cities, cheat fate for a season — but at the door of death they posted a dog, and even Herakles had to fetch him and bring him back.[^1]

There is a strange tenderness in Hesiod's portrait: the hound wags his tail for everyone going in. The boundary is not cruel; it is simply absolute. Every age re-hires him — Dante's tormentor, the Sibyl's sleeping obstacle, MIT's authentication daemon — because every ordered world needs a gate that opens one way, and needs to believe something tireless is watching it.

homeric-hymns.body:
Homer knows the hound but not yet his name. In Iliad 8 Athena recalls saving Herakles ‘when he went down to the house of the door-keeper Hades to bring the hound of hateful Hades up from Erebos’ — *kyna stygerou Aïdao*, ‘the hound of hateful Hades’, as office rather than proper name.[^1] Odyssey 11 shows the hero himself among the dead, recalling that he was sent ‘for the hound’. The definite article does all the naming: the underworld has one hound, and everyone knows which.

The Homeric Hymns proper never stage him. The Hymn to Demeter — the corpus's great underworld poem — dramatizes the descent and return of [[persephone|Persephonē]] with Hades' immortal horses but no watchdog at the door.[^2] The silence is instructive: in the hymn's theology the boundary is managed by decree and pomegranate seed, not by fangs. Kérberos belongs to the heroic-katabasis tradition, and it is Hesiod, not Homer, who first writes his name.

sources.citation: Homeric Hymn to Demeter, trans. Martin West, Loeb Classical Library (2003).

epithets.body:
The hound's titles track his offices:[^1]

- **The hound of Hades** (κύων Ἀίδαο) — Homer's periphrasis, his oldest title: not a name but an office, ‘Hades' dog’
- **Brazen-voiced** (χαλκεόφωνος) — Hesiod's epithet: the bark of bronze, fit for the one sound the dead must hear
- **Fifty-headed** (πεντηκοντάκαρηνος) — Hesiod's count, already hyperbole for monstrosity
- **Three-headed** — The classical settlement: Euripides' Heracles reports the three-bodied hound, and three heads became canonical for art and Rome
- **Hundred-headed** (*belua centiceps*) — Horace's inflation, the beast grown beyond counting in Roman imagination[^2]
- **The spotted one** — The comparative gloss: if the name is kin to Vedic *śárvara-* ‘variegated’, the hound's oldest epithet may be his name itself[^3]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 8.368; Hesiod, Theogony 311–312; Euripides, Heracles 24.
Lincoln, Bruce, Death, War, and Sacrifice (University of Chicago Press, 1991).

oracle-sites.body:
Kérberos kept no oracle and received no cult, but two places in the Greek world claimed his passage. At **Cape Tainaron** (modern Cape Matapan), the southern tip of the Mani, a cave in the cliff was pointed out as the mouth of Herakles' descent and ascent with the hound; Pausanias reports the local tradition beside the temple and sanctuary of Poseidon on the headland, one of the formal ‘gates of Hades’ of Greek geography.[^1]

The rival site lay at the other end of the Greek world: the **Acherusian promontory** near Herakleia Pontike on the Black Sea, where Xenophon's Ten Thousand, marching home in 400 BCE, passed ‘the Acherusian Chersonese, where they say Herakles descended for the dog Cerberus’, and measured the cavern at more than two stades deep.[^2] The two gates mark the two directions of Greek katabasis geography — the Peloponnesian gate of the heroes and the Pontic gate of the far shore — and both were working landmarks to the travellers who named them.

iconography.body:
Greek artists faced the problem of painting the unpaintable: how many heads fit on a vase? Their solution stabilized early — two or three canine heads on a lion-sized body, with serpents bristling from the mane, spine, and tail, and often a beard of snakes along the jaw.[^1] The standard scene is the abduction: Herakles in his lionskin drags the chained hound, Hermes or Athena in attendance, while Eurystheus flees into his storage jar — a composition beloved of Athenian black-figure in the later sixth century BCE and of the Laconian painters, whose tondo in the Cabinet des Médailles is among the earliest surviving images of the hound.[^1]

South Italian red-figure of the fourth century folded him into fuller underworld scenes, at the feet of Hades and Persephone enthroned — his office, not his capture. Roman art inherited the type: he crouches beside the enthroned Dis in mosaics and sarcophagi, and the Orpheus compositions of the Empire show him tamed at the edge of the listening animals, the one beast whose silence proves the song.[^2]

sources.citation: Boardman, John, Athenian Black Figure Vases (Thames and Hudson, 1974); LIMC s.v. Kerberos.
Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae (LIMC), vol. VI (Zürich: Artemis, 1992), s.v. Kerberos.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in the Greek alphabet as **Κέρβερος** — attested from Hesiod onward (8th–7th c. BCE), in the manuscript tradition of the Theogony and the later literary and scholastic witnesses; the script is written left-to-right.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Kérberos*, giving the normalized reading /ˈkér.be.ros/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Greek Κέρβερος is written with initial kappa (Κ), which Latin transliterated as C — the single substitution that produced the familiar *Cerberus*.
- The acute accent on the epsilon marks the stress on the first syllable; the penult is omicron (ο), which Latin rendered as u to fit its own declension (-us for Greek -ος).
- The name's deeper etymology is contested: the Indo-European proposal (cognate with Vedic *śárvara-*, ‘spotted’) competes with the Pre-Greek substrate analysis of Beekes.[^2]
- The Unicode restoration Kérberos is registrable in .com; the Greek-alphabet form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

sources.citation: Beekes, Robert, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Brill, 2010), s.v. Κέρβερος.
